ety.text: From Middle English fox, from Old English fox (“fox”), from Proto-West Germanic *fuhs, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz (“fox”), from Proto-Indo-European *púḱsos (“the tailed one”), possibly from *puḱ- (“tail”).

senses.d: Any member of the genus Vulpes; a true fox.
ex: A group of foxes is called a skulk.

senses.d: The red fox, a small carnivore (Vulpes vulpes) with red or silver fur.
ex: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
It was earliest morning, when even small trees cast long shadows and scarlet foxes trot denward through the dew like flecks of fire.

senses.d: Other canines that resemble true foxes, of the genera Cerdocyon, Lycalopex, Otocyon, and Urocyon.
The fur of a fox.
A fox terrier.
A flying fox.
The gemmeous dragonet, a fish, Callionymus lyra, so called from its yellow color.
A cunning person.
A physically attractive person, typically a woman.
ex: And Jerry was cute, you know, I liked him, but Frank was a total fox. And he was rougher than Jerry, you know, not so cultured.

senses.d: A person with reddish brown hair, typically a woman.
To trick, fool or outwit (someone) by cunning or ingenuity.
To sham, to dissemble.
ex: He was not foxing. No, no: he was sick really.

senses.d: To confuse or baffle (someone).
ex: This crossword puzzle has completely foxed me.

senses.d: To act slyly or craftily.
To cheat or rob.
To discolour paper. Fox marks are spots on paper caused by humidity. (See foxing.)
ex: The pages of the book show distinct foxing.

senses.d: To make sour, as beer, by causing it to ferment.
To turn sour; said of beer, etc., when it sours in fermenting.
To intoxicate; to stupefy with drink.
ex: I drank […] so much wine that I was almost foxed.

senses.d: To repair (boots) with new front upper leather, or to piece the upper fronts of.

grp.label: any of the species in the tribe Vulpini

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French renard, from Old French renart, the name of the fox in the medieval Roman de Renart. A Germanic personal name, from Frankish *Raginahardu, from Proto-Germanic *Raginaharduz, from *raginą (“counsel”) + *harduz (“hard, strong”).
Inherited from Latin vulpēs (accusative vulpem) from earlier volpēs, from Proto-Italic *wolpis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl(o)p ~ *h₂ulp (“(red) fox”).

First attested in the 15th century, chiefly in the feminine form zorra. Of unclear origin: * perhaps from Paleo-Hispanic. If so, it may be related to Spanish perro, * perhaps from Middle French sor (“yellowish-brown, reddish-brown, sorrel”), or * perhaps from Basque azeri (“fox”).

Inherited from Old Spanish raposo, probably from rabo (“tail”), itself from Latin rāpum (“turnip”). Probably influenced by Asturian rapiega (“fox”) or words related to rapiña and other derivatives of Latin rapiō (“snatch, grab”).

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese raposa, from Old Spanish raposa.

fr:piéger.gl: to trap (catch in a trap), to trick, to set up

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French piegier, from Old French piegier. By surface analysis, piège + -er.

it:ingannare.gl: to deceive, take in, mislead, hoodwink

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin ingannāre (attested in a gloss), from Latin ganniō. Compare Spanish engañar, Portuguese enganar.

fr:troubler.gl: to disturb, disrupt (order, sleep, judgement etc.)

ety.text: Inherited from Old French trobler, trubler, with metathesis from torbler, tourbler, turbler, from Vulgar Latin *turbulāre, itself either from Latin turbāre or from turbula, diminutive of turba. Compare Occitan trebolar, Romanian tulbura.
